task_1.title: Add reset_encoding APIs for xarray objects
task_1.description: Xarray 2023.4.0 adds convenience methods to clear persisted encoding metadata from Dataset and DataArray objects, with supporting Variable behavior, so users can discard inherited backend encoding before writing or appending modified data without changing the actual dataset contents.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that users can explicitly remove stored encoding metadata from xarray objects after loading or modifying data, so backend-specific encoding does not interfere with later writes, appends, or re-encoding workflows.

expectation.grounded: Provide `Dataset.reset_encoding()` and `DataArray.reset_encoding()` as public methods that return new objects with encoding cleared. Clearing must apply to the Dataset-level encoding, each contained variable and coordinate in a Dataset, and the DataArray data variable plus attached coordinates. `Variable.reset_encoding()` must likewise return a new Variable with empty encoding. These methods must preserve the represented data and structure while leaving the original object unchanged.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to call a dedicated reset API on loaded xarray objects to drop inherited encoding metadata and continue working with equivalent data using default or newly supplied encoding settings. The reset operation should behave like a non-destructive copy that removes encoding state but does not alter the actual contents of the object.

constraints.grounded: Resetting encoding must not mutate the original Dataset, DataArray, or Variable. The returned object must compare equal in data and coordinates to the source object aside from encoding state. All cleared encoding containers should become empty rather than partially preserved.
constraints.conceptual: The feature must be safe to use as a metadata cleanup step: it should only remove encoding information, keep the original object intact, and avoid changing values, dimensions, coordinates, or overall dataset meaning.

behavior: Calling `Dataset.reset_encoding()` returns a new Dataset whose own encoding is empty.
Calling `Dataset.reset_encoding()` clears encoding on every variable and coordinate contained in the returned Dataset.
Calling `DataArray.reset_encoding()` returns a new DataArray whose data variable encoding is empty.
Calling `DataArray.reset_encoding()` also clears encoding on attached coordinates in the returned DataArray.
Calling `Variable.reset_encoding()` returns a new Variable with empty encoding.
For all three object types, the source object retains its original encoding state after reset is called.
Resetting encoding does not change the underlying data, dimensions, coordinates, or equality of the returned Dataset relative to the source, apart from encoding metadata removal.
acceptance_criteria: When a Dataset has Dataset-level encoding and variable or coordinate encodings, calling `reset_encoding()` should return a Dataset with empty encoding at all of those levels.
When a DataArray has encoding on both the array and one or more coordinates, calling `reset_encoding()` should return a DataArray with empty encoding on the array and those coordinates.
When a Variable has encoding set, calling `reset_encoding()` should return a Variable whose encoding is empty.
When any reset method is called, the original object should still report its pre-existing encoding values afterward.
When comparing the original Dataset or DataArray to the reset result, they should remain equivalent in represented data and structure except for encoding metadata.

task_3.title: Support saving DataArray objects directly to Zarr
task_3.description: Version 2023.4.0 adds a direct `DataArray.to_zarr()` API so users can write `DataArray` objects to Zarr stores without first converting them to `Dataset`. The new behavior is designed to preserve round-trip loading for named and unnamed arrays, including cases where the array name conflicts with a dimension or coordinate name, and it supports the same deferred-write pattern exposed by the dataset-level Zarr writer.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that users can save an `xarray.DataArray` directly to a Zarr store, with the result remaining readable as the same data array shape, values, dimensions, coordinates, and name semantics after reopening.

expectation.grounded: `xarray.DataArray` should expose a public `to_zarr()` method that accepts the same Zarr persistence options exposed for dataset writes, including store selection, append and region settings, encoding, storage options, and `zarr_version`. Calling `DataArray.to_zarr()` should allow direct persistence to Zarr-backed stores and preserve round-trip behavior through `open_dataarray(..., engine="zarr")` for unnamed arrays, named arrays, and arrays whose name collides with a coordinate or dimension name. When `compute=False` is supplied, the method should return a `dask.delayed.Delayed` object instead of executing the data write immediately.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to write a single data array to Zarr directly, without converting it to another container type first. Reopening that store as a data array should reproduce the original array semantics, including edge cases around missing names and name conflicts. Deferred execution should also be available so writes can be scheduled and computed later.

constraints.grounded: The new capability must not regress existing `open_dataarray(..., engine="zarr")` behavior, including optional variable dropping on read. Direct Zarr writes must continue to support different store backends accepted by the Zarr interface, and the method's observable return type must remain `ZarrStore` for immediate writes and `dask.delayed.Delayed` for deferred writes.
constraints.conceptual: The feature should fit existing Zarr read and write workflows without changing how users reopen data arrays or use supported storage backends. Adding the convenience API must not break existing loading options or change the meaning of immediate versus deferred writes.

behavior: `DataArray.to_zarr()` is available as a direct persistence API for data arrays.
A data array can be written to a Zarr store without first converting it to a dataset.
Reopening a directly written unnamed data array through the Zarr engine yields an equivalent data array.
Reopening a directly written named data array through the Zarr engine yields an equivalent data array.
If a data array name matches one of its dimensions or coordinates, writing to Zarr and reopening it still preserves the original data array identity.
The Zarr-backed `open_dataarray()` path continues to honor read options such as dropping selected variables.
When `compute=False` is used, `DataArray.to_zarr()` returns a deferred object that writes successfully once computed.
acceptance_criteria: When a user calls `DataArray.to_zarr()` on an unnamed data array and reopens the target with `open_dataarray(..., engine="zarr")`, it should load as an equivalent data array.
When a user calls `DataArray.to_zarr()` on a named data array and reopens the target with `open_dataarray(..., engine="zarr")`, it should load as an equivalent data array.
When a data array name conflicts with a dimension or coordinate name, writing with `DataArray.to_zarr()` and reopening it should still preserve the original array semantics.
When `DataArray.to_zarr(..., compute=False)` is called, it should return a `dask.delayed.Delayed` object, and computing that object should complete the write successfully.
When a data array has extra variables that are excluded during `open_dataarray(..., engine="zarr", drop_variables=[...])`, the dropped variables should be omitted from the loaded result as expected.
When users write to supported Zarr store targets, direct data-array persistence should behave consistently across those store forms.

task_2.title: Refresh backend engine discovery after environment changes
task_2.description: Xarray 2023.4.0 adds a public way to refresh backend engine discovery so newly installed backend dependencies and entrypoint-based plugins can be recognized during the same Python session. This addresses cases where engine availability was cached too early and users otherwise had to restart their kernel before APIs such as `open_zarr()` or backend selection could see newly available engines.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that backend engine discovery can be refreshed at runtime so datasets using newly installed or newly registered engines are recognized in the current session without requiring a process or kernel restart.

expectation.grounded: Expose `xarray.backends.refresh_engines()` as a public API that invalidates the cached results of `xarray.backends.list_engines()`. After refresh, built-in backends such as `zarr`, `netcdf4`, `scipy`, `h5netcdf`, `pydap`, `pseudonetcdf`, `pynio`, and `store` must be re-evaluated against currently installed optional dependencies, and external backends discovered through the `xarray.backends` entry point group must be reloaded from the current environment. Engine-dependent APIs, including explicit engine selection and helpers such as `open_zarr()`, should then recognize engines that became available after the initial import instead of continuing to behave as if the old engine list were still active.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to install or expose an Xarray backend during an active session, call a refresh operation, and immediately have backend discovery reflect the new environment. After refreshing, operations that depend on backend availability should behave as though Xarray had been imported after the installation.

constraints.grounded: Refreshing engine discovery must only reset and rebuild backend availability and plugin registration state; it must not require a restart, and it must not permanently retain stale entrypoint-based engines from a previous cached result. Built-in engines should appear only when their optional dependency is currently importable, while the always-available store backend must remain present. Existing engine ordering and backend metadata discovery through `list_engines()` must remain intact after refresh.
constraints.conceptual: Refreshing should update backend visibility without changing unrelated dataset behavior. The refreshed engine list should match the current environment exactly, drop no-longer-available dynamic engines, preserve normal engine listing behavior, and keep always-supported backends available.

behavior: `xarray.backends.refresh_engines()` clears cached backend discovery state so the next `xarray.backends.list_engines()` call rebuilds the engine registry.
A backend installed after Xarray was first imported becomes visible in `list_engines()` after refresh, without restarting the interpreter.
A previously cached external backend entrypoint is replaced by the currently discoverable set after refresh rather than being merged with stale results.
Built-in backend visibility is determined at refresh time from the current availability of each optional dependency instead of a one-time class-level flag captured at import time.
The `store` backend remains available regardless of optional dependency changes.
acceptance_criteria: When a session imports Xarray before an optional backend dependency is installed, and that dependency is later installed, calling `xarray.backends.refresh_engines()` followed by `xarray.backends.list_engines()` should include the corresponding engine if the dependency is now importable.

When a session refreshes engine discovery after the set of registered `xarray.backends` entrypoints changes, `xarray.backends.list_engines()` should reflect only the currently registered plugins and should not retain plugins from the earlier cached result.

When code uses a backend-specific API such as `open_zarr()` after the relevant backend becomes available and engines are refreshed, the operation should no longer fail solely because Xarray is using a stale engine registry.
When optional backend dependencies are absent, `xarray.backends.list_engines()` should omit those engines while still including always-available backends such as `store`.

When `xarray.backends.list_engines()` is called repeatedly without a refresh, it may reuse cached discovery results; after `xarray.backends.refresh_engines()`, the next call should rebuild those results from the current environment.

task_5.title: Avoid unnecessary copies for exact alignment
task_5.description: The upgrade optimizes xarray alignment when callers request exact index matching with copy avoidance. When objects are already exactly aligned and `copy=False` is used, alignment should preserve the existing objects instead of performing redundant reindexing work, while keeping the exact-match behavior unchanged.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that exact alignment requests avoid unnecessary copying and reindexing work when inputs are already aligned, while preserving the existing exact-match contract and observable alignment behavior.

expectation.grounded: For `xarray.align` with `join="exact"` and `copy=False`, already-aligned inputs should be returned without reindexing into new aligned results. The public exact-join contract remains the same: alignment succeeds only when indexes already match exactly, and this optimization applies to aligned arrays and datasets across supported index types.
expectation.conceptual: When users ask for exact alignment without copying, the operation should behave like a zero-work pass-through for inputs that are already aligned. The upgrade should improve efficiency without changing whether exact alignment succeeds or fails.

constraints.grounded: The optimization must not alter `xarray.align` semantics for other join modes, must not weaken the validation behavior of `join="exact"`, and must not introduce reindexing or copies for already-aligned inputs when `copy=False`. Cases that are not exactly aligned must continue to follow existing exact-join behavior rather than being coerced into alignment.
constraints.conceptual: Only the performance characteristics should improve for the exact no-copy case. All compatibility checks, failure conditions, and behaviors for other alignment modes should remain unchanged.

behavior: Calling `xarray.align` with `join="exact"` and `copy=False` on objects that already share identical indexes should return aligned results without reindexing work.
The exact-join mode should continue to require identical indexes rather than reconciling differences.
Other join modes such as outer, inner, left, right, and override should keep their prior alignment behavior.
The optimization should apply to realistic aligned objects including dataset-variable combinations and supported calendar-backed time indexes.
acceptance_criteria: When two xarray objects are already exactly aligned and `xarray.align(..., join="exact", copy=False)` is called, it should complete without performing a copy-oriented reindexing step.
When inputs are not exactly aligned, `join="exact"` should continue to reject the mismatch instead of silently aligning them.
When `copy=False` is not requested, this change should not imply any new behavior beyond the existing alignment contract.
When other join modes are used, alignment results should remain consistent with their established behavior.

task_6.title: Preserve existing CFTimeIndex instances during index casting
task_6.description: The upgrade avoids rebuilding an index that is already a CFTimeIndex when xarray performs its index-casting logic. This reduces unnecessary copying while preserving the existing behavior of converting other object-dtype indexes to CFTimeIndex when appropriate.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2023.4.0 does not recreate or copy an index that is already a `CFTimeIndex`, while continuing to recognize and convert eligible object-dtype time indexes to `CFTimeIndex` where users expect CF calendar behavior.

expectation.grounded: When xarray applies its internal index-casting path to a non-empty `pandas.Index` with object dtype, it should skip conversion if the index is already a `xarray.coding.cftimeindex.CFTimeIndex`. For other eligible object-dtype indexes, xarray should still attempt to construct a `CFTimeIndex`, and if that conversion is not supported it should leave the original index unchanged rather than failing.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2023.4.0 should see the same CF-time semantics as before, but without unnecessary duplication when the input is already in the correct CF calendar index form.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the conversion gate for non-empty object-dtype indexes other than excluding existing `CFTimeIndex` instances from recasting. Preserve the fallback behavior where unsupported conversions do not raise new errors and instead retain the original index.
constraints.conceptual: The update should improve efficiency only. It must not alter which inputs are recognized as CF-time indexes, and it must not introduce new failures for indexes that cannot be converted.

behavior: Existing `CFTimeIndex` inputs are preserved instead of being wrapped into a new `CFTimeIndex` instance again.
Non-empty object-dtype indexes that are not already `CFTimeIndex` continue to be considered for CF-time conversion.
If CF-time conversion is unavailable or the input is not a valid CF-time index source, xarray leaves the original index as-is.
acceptance_criteria: When xarray receives an index that is already a `CFTimeIndex`, it should keep that index in CF-time form without recasting it.
When xarray receives a non-empty object-dtype index representing CF-time values but not already as `CFTimeIndex`, it should still expose CF-time index behavior after normalization.
When xarray receives a non-empty object-dtype index that cannot be converted to `CFTimeIndex`, it should continue operating with the original index rather than raising a new conversion error.
Upgrading from 2023.3.0 to 2023.4.0 should not change user-visible calendar indexing semantics, aside from avoiding unnecessary copying for already-correct `CFTimeIndex` inputs.

task_7.title: Accept all integer degree dtypes in xr.polyval
task_7.description: The update fixes xr.polyval so polynomial coefficient coordinates with valid NumPy integer dtypes are accepted consistently across platforms and dtype variants, instead of being rejected even though they represent integer polynomial degrees.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that xr.polyval accepts polynomial degree coordinates expressed with any valid integer dtype, so users can evaluate polynomial coefficients produced or stored with platform-specific or non-default integer types without spurious validation failures.

expectation.grounded: xr.polyval(coord, coeffs, degree_dim=...) should treat the coordinate on degree_dim as valid when its dtype is any NumPy integer subtype, including standard signed and unsigned integer variants such as int32, int64, and uint8. When the degree coordinate is integer-typed, polynomial evaluation should proceed normally and produce the expected numeric result. xr.polyval should continue to raise ValueError when the degree_dim coordinate is missing labels or when that coordinate is not of an integer dtype.
expectation.conceptual: Polynomial evaluation should work whenever degree labels are genuine integers, regardless of which concrete integer storage type was used. Users should only see validation errors for truly invalid degree labels, not for harmless integer dtype differences between platforms or datasets.

constraints.grounded: The change must remain limited to dtype acceptance for the degree coordinate used by xr.polyval. Existing validation that degree_dim is a labeled coordinate and that non-integer degree labels are rejected with ValueError must remain intact. Successful evaluations for already supported integer inputs must continue to behave the same.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must broaden valid integer inputs without weakening input validation overall. It must not change results for existing valid calls, and it must not allow non-integer degree labels to pass.

behavior: xr.polyval now accepts degree coordinates backed by integer dtypes beyond the platform default integer type.
Degree coordinates stored as int32, int64, or unsigned integer types are treated as valid polynomial degree labels.
Polynomial evaluation completes successfully for coefficients whose degree coordinate uses those integer dtypes.
Calls still fail with ValueError when the degree axis is not a coordinate with labels.
Calls still fail with ValueError when the degree coordinate dtype is not an integer type.
acceptance_criteria: When xr.polyval is called with coefficient degree labels stored as int64 integers, it should evaluate the polynomial and return the expected values.
When xr.polyval is called with coefficient degree labels stored as int32 integers, it should evaluate the polynomial and return the expected values.
When xr.polyval is called with coefficient degree labels stored as unsigned integers, it should evaluate the polynomial and return the expected values.
When xr.polyval is called with a degree axis that is not represented by labeled coordinates, it should raise ValueError.
When xr.polyval is called with degree labels that are not integer-typed, it should raise ValueError rather than evaluating.

task_4.title: Remove deprecated rasterio-backed opening APIs in favor of rioxarray
task_4.description: Version 2023.4.0 removes xarray's deprecated rasterio integration instead of continuing to ship it behind deprecation warnings. Code that previously opened raster datasets through xarray must migrate to the supported rioxarray-based workflow, and applications should no longer rely on xarray exposing rasterio-specific helpers, examples, or related compatibility behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading from 2023.3.0 to 2023.4.0 no longer depend on xarray's deprecated rasterio-opening APIs and instead treat geospatial raster loading through the supported external workflow as the required path.

expectation.grounded: In 2023.4.0, the deprecated public APIs `xarray.open_rasterio` and `xarray.tutorial.open_rasterio` are removed rather than emitting deprecation warnings. Users upgrading from 2023.3.0 must expect raster loading, raster tutorial dataset access, and related workflows that previously relied on xarray's rasterio backend semantics to stop being provided by xarray itself. The release note explicitly directs users to `rioxarray` as the supported replacement.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, xarray should no longer be expected to open raster files through its old built-in rasterio path. Any user workflow that needs raster dataset ingestion should be considered migrated to the supported external solution, and applications should treat the old xarray raster entry points as unavailable.

constraints.grounded: Do not preserve compatibility expectations around `xarray.open_rasterio` behavior, including its lazy raster indexing, optional coordinate parsing, raster metadata exposure, dask chunked reads, `WarpedVRT` handling, tutorial raster dataset download helper, or deprecation-warning-based fallback behavior. Non-raster xarray opening APIs remain outside the scope of this change.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should remove reliance on the retired raster convenience layer without changing unrelated dataset-opening behavior. Existing applications must not assume the old raster helper still exists, still warns, or still provides equivalent metadata and indexing behavior inside xarray.

behavior: Importing or calling `xarray.open_rasterio` is no longer a supported runtime path in 2023.4.0.
Importing or calling `xarray.tutorial.open_rasterio` is no longer a supported runtime path in 2023.4.0.
Raster examples and tutorial affordances previously documented through xarray are removed along with the deprecated backend.

Raster-specific behavior previously exposed through xarray's rasterio integration, such as generated `band`/`x`/`y` coordinates, raster metadata attributes, and rasterio-backed lazy indexing and chunking, should no longer be expected from xarray's own API surface.
The supported upgrade direction is to use `rioxarray` for raster I/O workflows that previously depended on xarray's deprecated rasterio backend.
acceptance_criteria: When an application is upgraded to xarray 2023.4.0, it should not rely on `xarray.open_rasterio` being importable or callable.
When an application is upgraded to xarray 2023.4.0, it should not rely on `xarray.tutorial.open_rasterio` being available for sample raster access.
When a raster-loading workflow is reviewed after upgrade, it should be expressed through the supported `rioxarray`-based approach rather than through xarray's removed rasterio entry points.

When validating the upgrade, no acceptance check should depend on xarray emitting a deprecation warning before performing raster reads, because the deprecated API has been removed instead of retained.
When validating non-raster data loading, existing xarray dataset-opening workflows should remain unaffected by this raster-specific removal.

task_8.title: Preserve permission errors during xarray backend detection
task_8.description: Upgrading from xarray 2023.3.0 to 2023.4.0 changes file-opening behavior so unreadable dataset paths no longer surface as generic backend-detection failures. When xarray auto-detects an IO engine for APIs such as open_dataarray, open_dataset, or open_mfdataset, permission-related read failures are now exposed directly as PermissionError, making the real access problem visible to users.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that opening a dataset or data array from a file path without read permission fails with a permission-related error instead of a generic backend-matching failure during IO engine detection.

expectation.grounded: When xarray selects an engine through backend guessing for file-based inputs, PermissionError raised while a backend checks whether it can open the target should propagate to the caller. Calls that rely on automatic engine detection, including open_dataarray, open_dataset, and open_mfdataset, should therefore expose PermissionError for unreadable files rather than converting the condition into a ValueError about no matching installed IO backend.
expectation.conceptual: If a file exists but the process is not allowed to read it, xarray should report that access is denied. Users should see a permission failure that reflects the real cause, not a misleading indication that no suitable file format backend is installed or matched.

constraints.grounded: Only permission-denied conditions encountered during backend guess_can_open checks should be re-raised directly. Normal backend probing should continue to tolerate other backend-specific exceptions for engine discovery, and successful engine detection for readable files must remain unchanged.
constraints.conceptual: The change should improve diagnosis of unreadable files without altering normal file-opening behavior for readable inputs or broadly changing how unrelated engine-detection errors are handled.

behavior: Automatic IO engine detection now preserves PermissionError raised while probing candidate backends against a file path.
Unreadable files no longer fall through backend probing and end in a generic no-matching-backend ValueError.
User-facing open calls that depend on engine guessing now fail earlier with a permission-denied signal when file access is blocked.
Backend guessing continues to ignore and warn on non-permission exceptions raised by candidate backends during compatibility checks.
acceptance_criteria: When a user calls an xarray open API with automatic engine detection on an existing file that lacks read permission, it should raise PermissionError.
When the same unreadable file is opened through an API path that previously reported no matching installed backend, it should no longer raise that backend-matching ValueError.
When a readable file is opened with automatic engine detection, xarray should continue selecting a compatible backend and opening the data as before.

When a candidate backend fails for reasons other than permission denial during engine probing, engine discovery should continue using existing fallback behavior rather than treating every probe failure as fatal.

task_9.title: Preserve provided BoundaryNorm behavior in DataArray plotting
task_9.description: The plotting upgrade corrects xarray's handling of caller-provided matplotlib BoundaryNorm instances so DataArray plots use the supplied normalization directly instead of rebuilding a discrete colormap configuration that can distort color mapping and colorbar behavior. This aligns xarray plots more closely with Matplotlib when discrete boundaries, over/under colors, and fixed norm ranges are used.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that DataArray plotting honors a user-supplied BoundaryNorm consistently so discrete color mapping and colorbar rendering match the intended normalization boundaries, including cases where the plotted data does not reach the norm's upper bound.

expectation.grounded: When DataArray.plot() and related 2D plot methods are called with a matplotlib.colors.BoundaryNorm via the norm parameter, xarray should preserve that BoundaryNorm instead of deriving a replacement discrete normalization from inferred levels. Observable plotting output, including contourf colorbar normalization, should remain consistent with the supplied boundary structure and with Matplotlib behavior.
expectation.conceptual: Plots that are given an explicit discrete normalization should respect it exactly. Users should see the same binning, color assignment, and colorbar semantics they asked for, without the library silently shifting or recomputing the normalization.

constraints.grounded: Providing explicit levels without a BoundaryNorm should continue to produce discrete colormap behavior. Passing a BoundaryNorm should not break existing plotting APIs, should continue to support colorbars, and should preserve observable handling of boundary counts, over/under ranges, and discrete contourf rendering.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must be additive and non-disruptive: existing discrete plotting workflows should keep working, while explicit normalization inputs should no longer be altered behind the scenes.

behavior: DataArray plotting methods use a caller-provided BoundaryNorm as the active normalization rather than rebuilding a separate discrete norm from levels.
Discrete color bins and colorbar intervals remain aligned with the supplied BoundaryNorm boundaries.
Plots with over/under colors or extended colorbars no longer shift their displayed mapping simply because the current data range does not include values beyond the norm limits.
Contourf plots using BoundaryNorm keep colorbar normalization metadata internally consistent with the discrete colormap configuration.
acceptance_criteria: When a DataArray is plotted with a supplied BoundaryNorm, the rendered color segmentation should follow that norm's boundaries rather than an inferred replacement.
When the same data, colormap, and BoundaryNorm are plotted through xarray and the corresponding Matplotlib plotting function, the resulting discrete color mapping should be consistent.

When a colormap defines over or under colors and the plotted data no longer contains values outside the BoundaryNorm range, the plot and colorbar should remain stable and should not shift bins unexpectedly.
When contourf is called with a BoundaryNorm, the resulting colorbar normalization should remain consistent with the number of colors and boundaries expected for that discrete norm.

task_10.title: Preserve reference-date timestamp formatting under pandas 2.0
task_10.description: The upgrade restores stable formatting for encoded time reference dates that fall outside pandas' nanosecond Timestamp range. Under pandas 2.0, these dates could be serialized with different year formatting, which changed dataset time-unit strings and broke round-trip expectations. The update keeps the user-visible encoding format consistent across supported pandas versions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that time encoding reference dates outside the nanosecond-precision datetime range continue to serialize with the same user-visible formatting after upgrading to pandas 2.0, so encoded units and round-tripped datasets remain stable.

expectation.grounded: When xarray formats reference dates for encoded time units through `format_timestamp`, values that can be represented by `pandas.Timestamp` should use a stable ISO-style datetime rendering rather than pandas' default string conversion. Values that raise `pandas.OutOfBoundsDatetime` must still fall back to the original object string representation. This preserves public-facing encoded unit strings such as CF-style time-unit references across backends and pandas versions.
expectation.conceptual: Time reference dates should keep the same visible string format before and after the dependency upgrade. Supported datetimes should serialize consistently, and dates outside pandas' supported range should still remain representable without changing existing observable behavior.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the successful handling of out-of-bounds datetime inputs beyond preserving their existing fallback behavior. Do not introduce different unit encodings for the same valid reference date solely because pandas changed its default timestamp string formatting. The fix should remain compatible with round-trip encoding behavior across storage backends that expose encoded time units.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should remove version-dependent formatting drift without altering how unsupported dates are surfaced. Existing datasets should continue to encode and decode time references consistently across supported storage formats.

behavior: Reference dates used in encoded time units retain consistent zero-padded year formatting for representable datetimes after upgrading pandas.
Formatting of supported timestamp-like inputs no longer depends on pandas' default string representation.
Inputs outside pandas' Timestamp bounds continue to be formatted through the non-Timestamp fallback path instead of failing.
Round-tripped datasets preserve the same visible time-unit reference strings across affected backends.
acceptance_criteria: When a dataset encodes time values using a reference date such as year 0001 that is still accepted by `pandas.Timestamp`, the resulting time-unit string should keep the same zero-padded date format as before the upgrade.
When the same dataset is round-tripped through supported xarray backends, the encoded time-unit reference string should remain unchanged under pandas 2.0.
When a reference date is outside the supported `pandas.Timestamp` bounds, formatting it should not raise due to this change and should continue using the established fallback representation.
When users upgrade from xarray 2023.3.0 to 2023.4.0, observable time encoding behavior for existing datasets should be stable apart from the removal of pandas-2.0-specific formatting regressions.

task_11.title: Support pandas 2.0 dtype and time-series behavior
task_11.description: The upgrade removes the effective pandas 2.0 compatibility barrier by aligning xarray's dtype-sensitive indexing, datetime accessors, resampling, and grouped binning behavior with newer pandas semantics. This preserves expected user-facing behavior while warning on unsupported float16 index usage and normalizing outputs where pandas changed defaults.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to the newer release allows applications to work with `pandas>=2.0` without breaking common xarray workflows involving coordinate selection, datetime field access, resampling, and bin-based grouping, while surfacing clear warnings or errors for unsupported dtype cases.

expectation.grounded: xarray should support `pandas>=2.0` by preserving observable behavior in `DataArray.sel`, datetime access via `.dt`, `resample`, and `groupby_bins`. When coordinates or selection labels involve `float16`, index construction and lookup should remain functional by coercing to a pandas-supported floating dtype and emitting a `DeprecationWarning` for `float16` index inputs. Datetime accessor fields such as `daysinmonth` and `days_in_month` should continue to return stable named `DataArray` results with consistent integer dtype rather than inheriting pandas 2.0's narrower integer output. `resample` should continue to match pandas-style aggregation semantics for standard and CFTime-backed date indexes, including support for `closed`, compatibility handling for deprecated `base` and `loffset` parameters, and validation of invalid `loffset` values. `groupby_bins` should preserve user-specified binning options such as interval closure and `include_lowest`.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, users should be able to adopt pandas 2.0 and still get the same practical xarray behavior for selection, date/time-derived fields, resampling, and binning. Unsupported low-precision index dtypes should not fail unpredictably; they should either work through safe coercion with a warning or raise a clear validation error when the input is invalid. Time-based operations should keep producing stable, predictable outputs across both regular pandas timestamps and calendar-aware time indexes.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing successful selection behavior for `float32` and `float64` coordinates, including scalar and vectorized label selection. Preserve monotonicity validation for `resample`. Keep deprecated `base` and `loffset` parameters behaviorally compatible with existing usage while still warning. Invalid `loffset` inputs must continue to raise `ValueError`. Grouped binning results must reflect the requested interval closure instead of default pandas assumptions. Datetime accessor outputs must remain dtype-stable and identity-stable for exposed field names and aliases.
constraints.conceptual: Existing working indexing and time-series operations should continue to behave the same for users who are not relying on unsupported dtypes. The upgrade must avoid silent behavior changes in grouping boundaries, output types, or calendar handling, and it must keep deprecation and validation signals visible where inputs are no longer directly supported.

behavior: Creating or using xarray indexes from `float16` coordinate data should succeed through safe coercion to a pandas-supported floating dtype and emit a `DeprecationWarning` instead of failing during index creation or label lookup.
Selecting data with floating-point coordinates should continue to work for `float32` and `float64` coordinates for both slice-like and scalar label selections.
Datetime accessor fields, including `daysinmonth` and `days_in_month`, should return consistent `DataArray` outputs with stable names and integer dtypes despite pandas 2.0 dtype changes.

Resampling over standard datetime indexes and CFTime-backed indexes should produce results consistent with pandas-style aggregation, including support for `closed="right"` and documented frequency examples.
Using deprecated resampling parameters such as `base` and `loffset` should still warn and produce the expected shifted or offset-aligned result rather than breaking under pandas 2.0 changes.
Supplying an invalid `loffset` value should continue to raise `ValueError` even when deprecation warnings are also emitted.
`groupby_bins` should honor explicit interval options such as left-closed bins and `include_lowest`, yielding intervals that match the user-requested boundaries.
acceptance_criteria: When a user upgrades to the new release with `pandas>=2.0`, coordinate selection with `float32` or `float64` coordinates should behave the same as before for scalar and multi-label lookups.
When a user creates or selects against `float16` coordinates, the operation should complete and emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating that the dtype is not natively supported for pandas indexes.
When a user accesses datetime-derived fields such as month-length information through `.dt`, the returned values should preserve xarray's expected output dtype and field naming conventions.

When a user resamples time-indexed data with standard datetime indexes or CFTime indexes, the aggregated results should match the expected bucket boundaries and labels for the requested frequency and closure settings.
When a user resamples with deprecated `base` or `loffset` arguments, the operation should emit a warning but still produce the corresponding offset-adjusted result.
When a user passes an invalid `loffset` value, the resampling operation should raise `ValueError` rather than silently accepting or misinterpreting it.
When a user performs `groupby_bins` with explicit bin closure settings, the output intervals and aggregated values should reflect those exact settings.

task_13.title: Clarify how to open different file formats as xarray datasets
task_13.description: The 2023.4.0 update adds FAQ guidance explaining how users should open different file formats as xarray datasets, centered on the use of xarray.open_dataset() and directing users toward the appropriate format support rather than changing runtime behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that users can determine how to open a given file format as an xarray dataset, including when to use xarray's standard dataset-loading API and when format support depends on other packages or backends.

expectation.grounded: The upgrade should document that opening file formats in xarray is done through the public API xarray.open_dataset(), and should clarify how users identify the appropriate format-specific support path for a target file type. This requirement is grounded in the release note evidence only; no code or test diff was provided to establish additional behavioral changes.
expectation.conceptual: Users should have clear, user-facing guidance for loading supported file formats into xarray without having to infer the correct entry point or guess whether extra format support is needed.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new runtime behavior, new error handling semantics, or new file-format support claims beyond what is documented for xarray.open_dataset() and its existing ecosystem integrations. Preserve the existing loading interface and frame the change as documentation and discoverability only.
constraints.conceptual: The update should improve clarity without changing how the library actually reads data or expanding support beyond what the product already provides.

behavior: The documentation should present xarray.open_dataset() as the primary user-facing entry point for opening dataset files.
The guidance should help users map a target file format to the appropriate xarray-supported loading path.
The update should clarify that some formats may rely on external backends or companion packages rather than a format-specific xarray API.
The change is documentation-facing and should not alter runtime loading behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a user looks up how to open a file format in xarray, the documentation should direct them to xarray.open_dataset() as the standard entry point.
When a file format requires backend-specific or external-package support, the guidance should make that dependency discoverable to the user.
When upgrading from 2023.3.0 to 2023.4.0, users should observe improved documentation for file-format loading without any expected change in dataset-opening behavior.
The documented guidance should reduce ambiguity about whether xarray itself or an ecosystem integration is responsible for opening a given format.

task_12.title: Preserve boolean dtype across encoded netCDF roundtrips
task_12.description: The 2023.4.0 update fixes boolean variable serialization so data saved and reloaded through xarray's CF/netCDF encoding pipeline keeps its boolean dtype across decode and subsequent re-encode cycles. This prevents boolean arrays from degrading when users persist data and then save the loaded result again.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that boolean-valued xarray data remains boolean after being saved and loaded through the library's encoding/decoding pipeline, including repeated roundtrips, so persisted data preserves its logical type and behavior.

expectation.grounded: When `DataArray` or `Dataset` variables with dtype `bool` are written through xarray's CF/netCDF serialization path and decoded back, the decoded variable should expose dtype `bool`, and its decoding metadata should retain enough information for a subsequent write/read cycle to keep the variable boolean again. The fix applies to the boolean handling performed by the library's encoding and decoding flow, including `BooleanCoder` and the stored `dtype` encoding metadata used during roundtrip serialization.
expectation.conceptual: Boolean data that users save and reopen should still behave as boolean data, not silently change type after loading or after saving the loaded result again.

constraints.grounded: The fix must preserve existing data values and roundtrip identity for boolean variables, must not require callers to manually set dtype metadata, and must not override cases where an explicit non-default dtype encoding or attribute was already supplied by the user. Non-boolean dtype handling should continue to follow the existing serialization rules.
constraints.conceptual: The change should only correct unintended loss of boolean type information, without changing the actual values, without adding new user configuration requirements, and without altering unrelated serialization behavior.

behavior: Boolean variables are encoded for storage in a way that can be decoded back to observable dtype `bool`.
Decoded boolean variables retain serialization metadata needed for later writes to preserve boolean dtype on another roundtrip.
A second save/load cycle of already-decoded boolean data yields the same boolean dtype and logical values as the original input.
If users already provide explicit dtype metadata, the library should respect that instead of applying the default boolean encoding path.
acceptance_criteria: When a user saves a `DataArray` containing boolean values and loads it back, the loaded array should report dtype `bool` and contain the same values.
When a user saves a `Dataset` containing a boolean variable, reloads it, and saves the reloaded result again, the second loaded result should still report dtype `bool` for that variable.
When boolean data is roundtripped through the CF/netCDF serialization path, the roundtripped object should remain logically identical to the original data.
When a variable is not boolean, or when explicit dtype metadata has already been provided by the user, serialization behavior should remain consistent with prior documented rules.

task_14.title: Preserve duck-array backend reads and lazy indexing semantics
task_14.description: The upgrade adds support for arrays read from storage backends that are array-like but not NumPy arrays, so xarray can preserve lazy or non-NumPy data during indexing, loading, formatting, and decoding. It also tightens backend indexing behavior so vectorized outer indexing and reversed slices remain shape-consistent when reading from Zarr-backed data.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that datasets opened from backends can expose and preserve non-NumPy duck arrays during lazy reads and loads, without forcing premature NumPy conversion, while keeping indexing, representation, and decoding behavior consistent for users.

expectation.grounded: When xarray opens data through BackendArray-based backends, lazy indexing wrappers and Variable.data should preserve the underlying duck array instead of assuming NumPy conversion via np.asarray. Operations such as .data access, .load(), lazy isel-based indexing, CF decoding, and array formatting should continue to work when the backend returns a duck array that does not implement NumPy coercion. Backend outer indexing for ZarrArrayWrapper should correctly support vectorized-style decomposition with slices, including reversed slices, and loaded results should retain correct sizes.
expectation.conceptual: Reading from a backend should work even when the backend provides a non-NumPy array type, such as a GPU or other duck array. Users should be able to inspect, lazily index, format, and load data without unexpected conversion failures, and indexed results should keep the expected shape and contents.

constraints.grounded: Do not require backend-returned arrays to be NumPy arrays in order for Variable.data, lazy wrappers, representation helpers, or load paths to succeed. Preserve duck-array types on load where possible, continue allowing explicit NumPy materialization only when requested through NumPy-facing paths, and avoid regressions in coordinate/index construction or dask-backed coordinate initialization. For backend indexing, reversed-slice and mixed outer-indexing cases must not produce size mismatches after load.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must broaden supported array types without breaking existing lazy behavior, shape consistency, or normal eager conversion paths. Existing workflows that depend on indexing, display, and loading should keep working, including edge cases involving reversed selections and computed coordinates.

behavior: Backend-backed variables may carry duck arrays through lazy indexing layers instead of being coerced to NumPy immediately.
Accessing .data on lazily opened variables should remain non-eager and compatible with non-NumPy backend arrays.
Calling .load() on a variable backed by a duck array should preserve the duck-array type rather than forcing NumPy conversion.
Elementwise decoding and masking paths should operate on duck arrays using their own array methods when possible.
Dataset and variable representations should format array content without assuming a NumPy ndarray source.
Zarr-backed outer indexing should correctly handle decomposed vectorized indexing with slices, including negative-step slices, so loaded subset sizes match lazy subset sizes.
Backends that naturally return NumPy arrays, such as pydap responses after fetch, should still normalize to NumPy where required for downstream shape handling.
Constructing datasets with dask-backed coordinate variables should not introduce extra compute passes.
acceptance_criteria: When a backend returns a duck array that raises on NumPy coercion, opening a dataset and accessing a variable's .data should not fail solely because of implicit NumPy conversion.
When such a variable is loaded, it should retain a duck-array data type rather than being converted to a NumPy ndarray.
When lazy selections are performed with .isel before load, they should remain valid for duck-array-backed variables and should not trigger unexpected eager data access.
When dataset or variable representations are generated for duck-array-backed data, the representation should succeed without requiring the array to be a NumPy ndarray.
When CF-decoded data uses scale or offset transformations, the decoded result should still work for duck-array-backed inputs.
Given a Zarr-backed dataset, when users apply outer indexing that includes slices and a reversed slice, the subset should report the same sizes before and after .load().
When coordinate data is backed by dask during dataset construction, the operation should not compute more than once.

task_15.title: Migrate GRIB reading to the external cfgrib backend plugin
task_15.description: The library removes its internal cfgrib-backed GRIB reader and relies on cfgrib's external backend entrypoint instead. Existing GRIB reads are intended to keep working through the same engine name when the cfgrib package is installed, while tutorial GRIB dataset access now fails fast with a direct import dependency error if cfgrib is unavailable.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that GRIB file access continues to work for users upgrading to 2023.4.0 by resolving the `cfgrib` engine through the external backend interface instead of the library's internal backend, and ensure that attempts to open GRIB-based tutorial datasets clearly fail when the `cfgrib` dependency is not installed.

expectation.grounded: Users should still be able to open GRIB data with `engine="cfgrib"` through xarray's backend plugin system when the external `cfgrib` package is installed and registered. The library should no longer expose or depend on internal `cfgrib` backend classes or include `cfgrib` among its built-in engine registry and built-in engine type hints. When tutorial dataset loading selects the `cfgrib` engine for `.grib` content and `cfgrib` cannot be imported, it should raise `ImportError` indicating that the `cfgrib` package is required.
expectation.conceptual: Upgrading should preserve the user-facing ability to read GRIB files through the `cfgrib` engine, but that support now comes from the separately installed backend plugin rather than from bundled internal integration. If the required GRIB reader dependency is missing, users should get an immediate and clear dependency error instead of ambiguous backend behavior.

constraints.grounded: The upgrade must not require users who already rely on the external `cfgrib` backend interface to change working GRIB read calls. Built-in backend discovery should continue to include standard internal engines while also loading external backend entrypoints without duplicate registration. This change must not imply continued public availability of internal symbols such as `CfGribDataStore` or built-in `cfgrib` engine membership in internal registries.
constraints.conceptual: Backward compatibility should be preserved for normal GRIB-reading workflows that already depend on the supported external backend package, while unsupported reliance on private bundled integration should no longer be assumed. Backend discovery should remain stable and predictable as external plugins are loaded.

behavior: GRIB reading support is provided via the external `cfgrib` backend entrypoint rather than an internal bundled backend implementation.
The engine name `cfgrib` remains the user-facing way to open GRIB data when the external backend package is installed.
Internal backend objects previously tied to bundled `cfgrib` support are removed from built-in backend exports and registries.
Opening tutorial datasets with a `.grib` suffix auto-selects `cfgrib` and now performs an explicit dependency check before proceeding.
If `cfgrib` is not installed, tutorial GRIB dataset loading raises `ImportError` instead of silently relying on internal backend availability.
Backend engine construction now combines built-in engines with external entrypoints in a way that supports plugin-based backend loading.
acceptance_criteria: When a user opens a GRIB dataset with `engine="cfgrib"` in an environment where the external `cfgrib` backend is installed, it should continue to open successfully after upgrading.
When a user loads an xarray tutorial dataset backed by a `.grib` file without explicitly setting an engine, the library should choose `cfgrib`.
When a user loads that tutorial GRIB dataset without `cfgrib` installed, it should raise `ImportError` describing that the `cfgrib` package is required.
When backend plugins are discovered, externally registered backends should be included alongside built-in engines without duplicate built-in registration of `cfgrib`.
When users depend only on documented GRIB-reading behavior rather than private backend classes, the upgrade should preserve expected runtime behavior.

task_16.title: Preserve CF variable coding behavior through dedicated VariableCoders
task_16.description: The 2023.4.0 update moves remaining CF encode/decode logic into dedicated VariableCoders while preserving user-visible conventions behavior. The upgrade formalizes handling for boolean variables, non-native endian arrays, default float fill values, non-string dtype encoding, and fill-value interactions so CF serialization and deserialization continue to produce consistent observable results.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2023.4.0 preserves the observable CF encoding and decoding behavior of variables while the implementation is moved into dedicated VariableCoders, including correct handling of booleans, non-native endian arrays, dtype coercion, and fill values.

expectation.grounded: CF encoding and decoding should continue to apply the same public xarray conventions after the VariableCoders migration. `encode_cf_variable` should use coder-based handling for non-string `encoding['dtype']` coercion, automatic `_FillValue` insertion for floating dtypes, and boolean serialization by recording `dtype='bool'` and storing data as integer bytes when no explicit dtype override is supplied. `decode_cf_variable` should preserve original decoded dtype metadata, convert non-native-endian arrays to native endianness when endianness decoding is enabled, and restore variables marked with `dtype='bool'` to boolean arrays while moving that dtype marker into encoding for subsequent re-encoding. `CFMaskCoder.encode` should treat `_FillValue` and `missing_value` independently, reject conflicting values when both are present, and only apply `missing_value`-based filling when `_FillValue` is absent.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade must keep CF read/write behavior stable for users: variables should still round-trip with the same effective types and missing-data semantics, boolean fields should decode back to booleans, endian conversion should still produce arrays usable as native machine types, and fill-value handling should remain predictable and reject contradictory metadata.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce behavioral regressions in `encode_cf_variable` or `decode_cf_variable` relative to prior CF conventions. Floating variables without explicit `_FillValue` or `missing_value` should still gain a default NaN fill value during encoding. Integer dtype coercion requested through `encoding['dtype']` must still round floating input and emit a `SerializationWarning` when floating data is saved as an integer dtype without any fill value metadata. Boolean auto-encoding must only occur when neither attrs nor encoding already specify `dtype`. Endianness conversion must remain lazy and only occur for non-native dtypes when endianness decoding is requested.
constraints.conceptual: The refactor must not change accepted inputs, round-trip expectations, warning conditions, or failure cases that users already rely on. Explicit metadata should continue to take precedence over automatic conversions, and automatic normalization should only happen when the prior behavior already implied it.

behavior: Boolean variables without an explicit dtype override are encoded as byte-valued storage with boolean dtype metadata and decode back to boolean arrays.
Variables marked as boolean by CF metadata restore boolean array semantics during decoding and retain enough dtype metadata to re-encode consistently.
Non-native-endian decoded arrays are exposed as native-endian arrays when endianness decoding is enabled.
Encoding with a target non-string dtype still coerces data to the requested dtype, including rounding when converting floating data to integer storage.
Encoding floating data to an integer dtype without `_FillValue` or `missing_value` still emits a serialization warning because NaN values would lack a sentinel.
Floating variables without an explicit fill value still receive a default NaN `_FillValue` during encoding.
If both `_FillValue` and `missing_value` are present and disagree, encoding fails with a `ValueError`.
If only `missing_value` is present, it is used for filling missing data; if `_FillValue` is present, that value takes precedence for filling.
acceptance_criteria: When a boolean variable is encoded without explicit dtype metadata, it should serialize using CF-compatible integer storage and decode back as a boolean variable.
When a decoded variable carries boolean dtype metadata, it should be exposed to users as boolean data rather than integer data.
When a variable contains non-native-endian data and endianness decoding is enabled, the decoded variable should expose native-endian dtype behavior.
When `encoding['dtype']` requests a different non-string dtype, encoding should coerce to that dtype and preserve scalar cases such as 0-dimensional integers.
When floating data is encoded to an integer dtype without any fill-value metadata, a `SerializationWarning` should be raised.
When a floating variable has no explicit `_FillValue`, encoding should supply a default NaN `_FillValue`.
When `_FillValue` and `missing_value` are both present with different values, encoding should raise `ValueError` instead of silently choosing one.
When only `missing_value` is present, missing data should be filled from it; when `_FillValue` is also present, `_FillValue` should control the fill operation.

task_18.title: Preserve nanosecond timestamp semantics during pandas 2.0 upgrade
task_18.description: The 2023.4.0 update adds a compatibility layer for pandas 2.0 so xarray continues to use nanosecond-precision timestamps in internal datetime-sensitive operations. This avoids incorrect or unstable behavior in decoding, encoding, calendar conversion, and related time-based workflows while broader support for non-nanosecond pandas datetimes remains deferred.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to pandas 2.0 does not change xarray's internal datetime behavior by continuing to treat nanosecond precision as the supported internal timestamp contract in precision-sensitive operations.

expectation.grounded: Under pandas 2.0 and later, xarray should normalize internally constructed `pd.Timestamp` values to nanosecond precision in datetime-sensitive paths, including CF datetime decoding and encoding, datetime unit inference, `cftime_to_nptime`, calendar conversion helpers, and `date_range_like` handling for NumPy datetime-like sources. `CFTimeIndex.to_datetimeindex` and downstream conversions should continue to yield nanosecond-based datetime results rather than incorrect shifted values. Public documentation and errors referring to bounds should describe the limit as the nanosecond-precision range rather than a generic `Timestamp` range.
expectation.conceptual: The library should preserve its existing time semantics across the pandas 2.0 upgrade by coercing internal timestamp handling back to nanosecond precision anywhere xarray relies on that assumption. Users should see stable datetime decoding, encoding, resampling, conversion, and calendar-related behavior, while expanded support for non-nanosecond pandas datetimes is not yet part of this release.

constraints.grounded: This change must be compatibility-preserving and conservative: it should not claim general support for non-nanosecond pandas datetime indexes, should keep nanosecond-based outputs and range checks in precision-sensitive APIs, and should continue raising existing datetime-related exceptions such as invalid-date or out-of-bounds failures where nanosecond precision cannot represent the value. Existing datetime workflows that surface pandas conversion warnings may still warn, but behavior should remain correct.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should favor correctness and continuity over new datetime capabilities. It must avoid silently changing supported ranges, calendar conversion rules, or time-based operation results, and it should not introduce a promise that arbitrary pandas datetime precisions now work throughout the library.

behavior: Internal timestamp construction in pandas-backed datetime code paths is coerced to nanosecond precision when running with pandas 2.0+.
CF datetime decoding and encoding continue to interpret reference dates using nanosecond-precision timestamps.
Datetime unit inference continues to choose reference timestamps under the nanosecond-precision assumption.
`cftime_to_nptime` continues to produce `datetime64[ns]` results and avoids bogus converted dates caused by non-nanosecond pandas timestamps.
Calendar conversion helpers that receive `pd.Timestamp` inputs continue to behave as if timestamps are nanosecond-precision values.
`date_range_like` continues to derive start and end bounds from NumPy datetime-like sources using nanosecond-precision timestamps.
Documentation and user-facing bounds language now describe failures in terms of the nanosecond-precision range.
acceptance_criteria: When xarray runs with pandas 2.0 or newer, datetime-sensitive internal operations should produce the same nanosecond-based observable results expected before the pandas upgrade.
When converting `CFTimeIndex` values to pandas-backed datetimes, the result should not contain nonsensical shifted dates introduced by precision mismatches.
When xarray decodes or encodes CF datetimes, reference-date handling should remain stable and nanosecond-based.

When time-based APIs such as resampling or calendar-aligned date range creation operate on supported datetime inputs, they should continue to return correct results rather than changing semantics because pandas now permits broader datetime precision.
When a datetime value is invalid or outside the representable nanosecond range, the operation should continue to fail in the established way rather than silently producing an incorrect timestamp.
User-visible documentation and bounds descriptions should reflect that the operative limitation is the nanosecond-precision range, not a blanket `Timestamp` limitation.

task_17.title: Add first-time contributor welcome bot messaging
task_17.description: The upgrade adds repository welcome-bot behavior for new contributors. First-time issue authors, first-time pull request authors, and users whose first pull request is merged should receive automated onboarding or celebration comments, improving contributor guidance without changing the library's runtime APIs.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that first-time GitHub contributors receive automated welcome messaging when they open their first issue, submit their first pull request, or have their first pull request merged.

expectation.grounded: The repository should define welcome-bot configuration that triggers automated comments for three first-time contribution events: a user's first issue, a user's first pull request, and the merge of a user's first pull request. The change is limited to contributor-facing GitHub automation and does not introduce or alter xarray runtime APIs.
expectation.conceptual: New contributors should be greeted automatically at the key moments of their first contribution so they receive onboarding guidance and recognition without any manual maintainer action.

constraints.grounded: The behavior should apply only to first-time contribution events, should produce automated comments as the observable outcome, and should not affect package execution, data model behavior, public Python APIs, or non-first-time contributor workflows.
constraints.conceptual: The enhancement should improve contributor onboarding only, without changing normal library behavior for users or creating repeated welcome messages for routine repeat contributions.

behavior: When a GitHub user opens their first-ever issue in the repository, the repository posts an automated welcome comment.
When a GitHub user opens their first-ever pull request in the repository, the repository posts an automated welcome comment.
When a GitHub user's first pull request is merged, the repository posts an automated congratulatory comment.
The update affects repository contribution workflow only and has no direct runtime effect on xarray consumers.
acceptance_criteria: When a first-time contributor opens an issue, it should automatically receive a welcome comment.
When a first-time contributor opens a pull request, it should automatically receive a welcome comment.
When a contributor's first pull request is merged, it should automatically receive a merge-congratulation comment.
When an existing contributor opens additional issues or pull requests after their first ones, the first-time welcome behavior should not be required to trigger again.
Upgrading to this version should not change any library runtime API or computation behavior for package users.
